notes.meaning: Joshua sent two scouts in secret across the Jordan to gather information about Jericho and its defenses. Taking sensible precautions did not show a lack of trust in God's promises, but showed wisdom in carrying out God's work. The scouts ended up at Rahab's house, an inn where travelers could stay without drawing too much attention. God guided their steps directly to the one person in Jericho ready to welcome them.

Jericho's guards were on high alert because Israel was camped just across the river. The scouts likely stood out by their speech or clothing, and local watchmen quickly spotted them. The king received word right away that enemy scouts had arrived in the city that night.

The king sent orders directly to Rahab's house, demanding that she hand over her foreign guests. He assumed she would remain loyal to her own city and do what she was told. Even when people know God is working, they often try to rely on their own political power to resist Him.

Rahab had already acted before the king's messengers arrived. Guessing that a search was coming, she hid the two men and told the messengers that the visitors had already departed. She risked her own life to protect God's people because she believed in the God of Israel.

differ.view: Some Baptists note that while Rahab's lie was wrong, it is explained by her pagan background, and God would have protected the spies even without her deception.

notes.meaning: Rahab gave the officers false directions, telling them the strangers slipped out just before the city gates closed for the night. She urged the king's men to chase after them quickly so they would leave her house right away. Her quick thinking sent the search party away in the wrong direction and bought time for the scouts.

notes.meaning: Flat rooftops in the ancient world were useful living spaces, often used for drying crops in the sun. Rahab had laid out harvested stalks of flax on her roof to dry so the fibers could be made into linen. The thick piles of stalks made a natural hiding spot where the spies could lie unseen.

The king's soldiers rushed toward the shallow places where people could cross the Jordan River, expecting to catch the scouts there. As soon as the pursuers marched out, the heavy city gates were locked tight behind them. This was meant to trap any remaining enemies inside, but it also showed the rising panic in the city.

As darkness fell and the scouts prepared to rest on the roof, Rahab came up to talk with them. The danger from the king's soldiers had passed for the moment. This quiet time gave her the opportunity to speak from the heart about what she believed.

Rahab made an astonishing statement of faith, declaring that she knew the LORD had already given Canaan to Israel. She told the spies that a deep dread had fallen over Jericho, leaving everyone paralyzed with fear. Her words showed that God's earlier promise to strike fear into Israel's enemies was coming true.

The people of Jericho had heard how the LORD dried up the Red Sea when Israel left Egypt forty years earlier. They had also heard how Israel recently wiped out the powerful Amorite kings, Sihon and Og, east of the Jordan. These mighty acts proved to the Canaanites that Israel's God possessed supreme power in battle.

Hearing of God's power drained the courage of everyone in the city, making their hearts melt with terror. Rahab went further than mere terror; she confessed that the LORD is the one true God over both heaven and earth. By turning away from the idols of her people, she placed her trust in the living God.

Rahab asked the spies to swear a solemn oath in the name of the LORD to protect her family. She pointed to the loyalty and kindness she had just shown them as a reason to show kindness in return. She also asked for a reliable sign that would guarantee their agreement.

Rahab specifically pleaded for the lives of her father, mother, brothers, and sisters, along with their families. She understood that total destruction was coming upon Jericho and begged that her family be rescued from death. Her plea showed deep love for her relatives and a desire that they share in her salvation.

The scouts pledged their own lives as a guarantee that Rahab and her family would be kept safe. They agreed to treat her with faithfulness and mercy when God delivered the city into Israel's hands. The only condition was that she must not reveal their mission or break their secret agreement.

Rahab helped the men escape by lowering them through a window with a sturdy rope. Because her house was built directly into the outer city wall, the window opened straight out to the countryside. This allowed the men to slip away safely while the city gates were locked.

Rahab gave the scouts smart advice to head west into the rugged limestone hills rather than east toward the Jordan. The hills were full of caves where they could easily hide from search parties for three days. Once the pursuers gave up the search and went home, the scouts could safely journey back to their camp.

The spies explained the terms that would keep their promise binding before God. They wanted to make sure neither side misunderstood what was required for protection. If the conditions were not kept, the scouts would be completely free from their oath.

The scouts gave Rahab a clear sign to display: she had to tie a bright scarlet cord in her window. She also had to gather all her family members inside her house before the Israelite army arrived. The bright cord would allow Israel's soldiers to spot her home easily and leave it unharmed.

The scouts warned that anyone who stepped outside the door into the street would lose the promise of safety and bear the blame for their own death. But if anyone was harmed while staying inside the house, the scouts agreed that the guilt would fall entirely on Israel. Safety depended on remaining sheltered under the roof marked by the pledge.

The scouts repeated that Rahab must keep their arrangement completely secret. If she told others about their mission, anyone could claim the same protection or try to ruin Israel's plans. Secrecy protected both the lives of the scouts and the safety of her family.

Rahab fully accepted their terms and sent the scouts on their way in peace. She then tied the scarlet cord in the window so the marker of rescue was ready. Her quick action showed her complete trust in the agreement and her readiness for God's deliverance.

The scouts followed Rahab's advice and hid in the caves of the nearby hills for three days. Meanwhile, the king's soldiers searched the roads all the way to the Jordan River without finding any trace of them. After the exhausted pursuers gave up and returned to Jericho, the scouts were safe to move.

The two men came down from the mountains, crossed over the Jordan River, and returned safely to the camp at Shittim. They reported everything that had happened to Joshua, including their escape and Rahab's confession. Their safe return proved God's protection and guidance over the whole expedition.

The scouts brought back a joyful report, declaring that the LORD had already given the entire land into Israel's hands. Unlike the fearful spies forty years earlier, these men saw that the inhabitants of Canaan were melting in terror. Their faith-filled words encouraged Joshua and the whole nation to move forward boldly in God's promises.
